title: 是 (shì) — To Be
explanation: 是 (shì) is the main verb 'to be' in Chinese. It connects a subject to a noun. Unlike English, it is NOT used with adjectives — use 很 (hěn) for adjectives instead.

title: 有 (yǒu) — To Have / There Is
explanation: 有 (yǒu) means 'to have' or 'there is/are'. Its negative form is 没有 (méiyǒu), NEVER 不有. Use 有 for possession and existence.

examples.en: There are apples on the table.

title: 不 (bù) — Negation
explanation: 不 (bù) negates most verbs and adjectives. Its tone changes to 2nd tone (bú) before 4th-tone syllables. Exception: use 没 (méi) to negate 有 and past actions.

title: 吗 (ma) — Yes/No Questions
explanation: Add 吗 (ma) to the end of any statement to make it a yes/no question. No word order change needed — unlike English, Chinese keeps the same sentence structure.

title: 的 (de) — Possessive / Modifier
explanation: 的 (de) marks possession (like 's in English) and connects adjectives/phrases to nouns. Between close family or pronouns, 的 is often omitted.

title: 了 (le) — Completed Action
explanation: 了 (le) after a verb marks a completed action (not past tense — it's about completion). 了 at the end of a sentence can also indicate a change of state.

title: 在 (zài) — Location
explanation: 在 (zài) means 'to be at/in' a location. Place it before the main verb to say where an action happens: Subject + 在 + Place + Verb.

examples.en: The book is on the table.

title: 想 (xiǎng) — Want to / Would like to
explanation: 想 (xiǎng) expresses desire to do something ('want to'). It is a modal verb — place it directly before the main verb. It also means 'to think/miss someone'.

examples.en: She wants to go to China.
What do you want to eat?
